course.title: Electronics Foundations
course.description: Work out how simple direct-current circuits behave, using diagrams you can change and calculations you can check.
course.audience: A beginner using an Arduino starter kit or studying introductory electricity.

paragraphs: Electronics is the study of how electric charge is made to do useful work in circuits. It sits behind torches, phone chargers and every board in an Arduino starter kit, and people study it to build gadgets of their own and to understand why a part burns out when it is connected the wrong way round.

The course has five lessons that build on each other, all using low-voltage direct current from a battery or a USB supply. The first follows the current round a single loop and introduces Ohm's law. Two lessons then add a second resistor, one in series and one in parallel. The fourth looks at the energy a circuit moves each second, and the last turns to parts such as the LED that do not follow Ohm's law, ending with the resistor that keeps an LED safe.
Each lesson explains an idea first and asks about it afterwards. Numbers are part of the work, so keep a calculator nearby.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the current in a loop from its voltage and resistance, using Ohm's law.
You'll be able to find the total resistance of a series circuit and the voltage across each part.
You'll be able to find the current in each branch of a parallel circuit and its equivalent resistance.
You'll be able to work out the power of a component and the energy it transfers in a given time.
You'll be able to choose the resistor that sets the current through an LED.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with decimals and division; no electronics is assumed.

lessons.title: Current in a single loop

steps.headline: What flows round a circuit

lead.text: Go back to the water loop. A flow meter on the pipe would count the litres that pass it each second. A copper wire is similar. It is full of tiny particles that carry electric charge and are free to drift along the metal. Join the two ends of a battery with a wire and the battery pushes that charge round the loop.

This flow of charge is called electric current. Where you counted litres each second in the pipe, here you count the charge that passes a point each second. Charge is measured in coulombs, and a current of one coulomb each second is one ampere, written 1 A. A small torch bulb takes about 0.3 A.
Current is a rate, like speed or litres per second, and it is the first number we need to describe any circuit. The next thing to find out is what happens to the flow when something gets in its way.

steps.headline: The same current at every point

lead.text: Something that gets in the way of the flow is called a resistor. It is a small part, often a little cylinder with a wire coming out of each end, and its job is to hold the flow back, like the narrow neck in the pipe. Put one in the loop and ask what a meter would read on each side of it.

A loop of wire is a single path. Charge that enters one end of the resistor has to leave by the other, because it has nowhere else to go and nowhere to be stored. If more charge left each second than entered, the resistor would be making charge from nothing. If less left, charge would pile up inside it. Neither can happen, so the same amount of charge passes every point of the loop each second.

People often expect the resistor to use up some of the current, the way a bulb seems to use up a battery. The current is smaller everywhere in the loop than it would be without the resistor, but it has the same size on both sides. That rule holds for any circuit made of a single path.

reveal.text: The same. Charge cannot vanish or pile up inside the resistor, so both meters agree.

steps.headline: What pushes the charge: voltage

lead.text: In the water loop the pump is what makes the water move. In a circuit that job belongs to the battery, and the size of its push is called voltage. Voltage is measured in volts, written V. A bigger voltage pushes harder, so the same part carries more charge each second.

Voltage is always a push between two points, here the two ends of the battery. A AA cell gives 1.5 V and the square 9 V battery gives 9 V, so the 9 V battery pushes six times as hard. Every circuit in this course runs on low voltages like these, from batteries or a USB supply.

A push alone does not settle how much flows. Two loops can have the same battery and still carry very different currents, depending on what is in the way. That second ingredient needs a name of its own.

steps.headline: What holds the charge back: resistance

lead.text: The name for how strongly a part holds the flow back is resistance. It is measured in ohms, written with the Greek capital omega, Ω. In the water picture a thin neck has a high resistance and a wide pipe has a low one. A 200 Ω resistor holds the flow back twice as strongly as a 100 Ω one.

That gives us three quantities to keep apart. The voltage is the push and the resistance is the hold-back. The current is what results: how much charge gets through each second. More push means more current, and more resistance means less. With the same 5 V battery, a 250 Ω resistor lets through less current than a 100 Ω resistor, because the same push meets a stronger hold-back.
To get actual numbers we need an exact rule that links the three. The German physicist Georg Ohm found one in the 1820s, and it is simple enough to use in your head.

steps.headline: Ohm's law: current from voltage and resistance

lead.text: Ohm's law says that the current equals the voltage divided by the resistance. In symbols it is I = V ÷ R, where I is the current in amperes, V is the voltage in volts and R is the resistance in ohms. Volts divided by ohms come out in amperes, which gives you a quick check that you have the equation the right way up.

Try it with 9 V across 90 Ω. The current is 9 ÷ 90 = 0.1 A. Double the voltage to 18 V and the current doubles to 0.2 A, because there is more push against the same hold-back. Go back to 9 V and double the resistance to 180 Ω, and the current halves to 0.05 A. Voltage sits on top of the division and resistance underneath, so one raises the current and the other lowers it.

Ohm's law works for resistors, where doubling the voltage doubles the current. Later in the course we meet parts that break that pattern. For now every part follows it, and the next screens put numbers through the equation.

stageTitles.review: Recall what a single loop does

blocks.text: Fill a loop of pipe with water and fit a pump into one side of it. Switch the pump on and the water starts to circulate. Halfway round, the pipe narrows to a thin neck. You might expect water to pile up behind the neck, or to arrive thinner on the far side. Neither happens. Count the litres passing a mark before the neck and a mark after it, and the two counts agree, because a closed pipe has nowhere to lose water and nowhere to store it.

A battery, a loop of wire and a small part that holds the flow back behave in the same way. The battery plays the pump and the part plays the narrow neck. Describing that loop in numbers is the first step to understanding every circuit in a torch, a phone charger or an Arduino kit.

We follow the flow once round the loop. First we say what is flowing and how to count it. After that we meet what pushes it and what holds it back, and one short equation turns those into a number you can check with a meter.

lessons.title: Resistance in series

steps.headline: Resistors on a single path

lead.text: Take the loop from the last lesson and add a second resistor straight after the first. The wire now runs from the battery through one resistor and then the other before it returns to the battery. Parts joined end to end like this are in series. A water pipe with two narrow necks one after the other is the same arrangement.

A series circuit has only one path for the charge, so the rule from last lesson applies to the whole loop. The same current passes through every part, whatever its resistance. A meter beside the first resistor and a meter beside the second will agree, just as the two meters on either side of a single resistor did.
The battery pushes against both resistors together, so the current depends on both of them. The next screen shows how their two values combine.

steps.headline: Resistances in series add

lead.text: Charge going round a series loop has to push through the first resistor and then through the second, so the hold-back builds up along the way. The two resistors together hold the flow back as strongly as one resistor whose resistance is the sum of theirs.

We call that sum the total resistance of the loop, and write it R = R₁ + R₂. A 100 Ω resistor followed by a 150 Ω resistor behaves like one 250 Ω resistor. A third resistor in the chain would add its own value as well, so a longer chain has a larger total than any single part in it.

Once the total is known, last lesson's rule does the rest. The battery's voltage divided by the total resistance gives the current for the whole loop. A 9 V battery across 250 Ω, for example, drives 9 ÷ 250 = 0.036 A through every part of the chain.

steps.headline: The voltage across one resistor

lead.text: The current is the same in both resistors, yet the battery's voltage has to go somewhere. Each resistor takes a part of it. The voltage measured across the two ends of one resistor is called the voltage drop across it, and Ohm's law tells you its size.

Ohm's law says I = V ÷ R, and the same equation can be read the other way round: V = I × R. The voltage across a resistor is the current through it times its own resistance. Take the 9 V loop with a 100 Ω and a 200 Ω resistor, where the current is 0.03 A. The 100 Ω resistor has 0.03 × 100 = 3 V across it, and the 200 Ω resistor has 0.03 × 200 = 6 V.
The two drops, 3 V and 6 V, add up to the battery's 9 V. That always happens, and the next screen shows why.

steps.headline: How the battery's voltage is shared

lead.text: Think of the battery as giving the charge a fixed amount of push for the trip round the loop. Each resistor takes some of that push away, and by the time the charge is back at the battery none is left. So the voltage drops around a series loop always add up to the battery's voltage.

Because the current is the same everywhere, the drop across a resistor depends only on its resistance. A resistor with twice the resistance takes twice the share, as the 200 Ω resistor took 6 V against 3 V for the 100 Ω one. The larger resistance always takes the larger share.

That gives a quick way to find a missing voltage. If a 6 V battery drives two resistors and one has 2 V across it, the other has 6 − 2 = 4 V. The same idea will help us size the resistor that protects an LED in the last lesson.

Now take a second 100 Ω resistor and join it into the same loop, one after the other, so that the charge has to get through both. The battery is the same as before, yet a meter on the wire will read a different number.

Circuits are full of parts that share one path, such as the bulbs on a string of old-fashioned fairy lights. Knowing how such parts combine lets you predict the current in a whole loop from the values printed on its components.
We follow the charge once round the longer loop. First comes the way the resistances combine, which gives the current. After that we see how the battery's push is shared out between the parts.

lessons.title: When a circuit splits into branches

steps.headline: Branches share one pair of connection points

lead.text: When a circuit splits into separate routes, each route is a branch. Parts on different branches are said to be in parallel. In the simplest case a branch is a single resistor, with one end wired to one end of the battery and the other end wired to the other end of the battery.

That wiring decides a great deal. The battery's push is measured between its two ends, and both branches are connected across those same two points. So each branch has the full battery voltage across it, exactly as if the other branch were not there. A 6 V battery puts 6 V across every branch you connect to it.

Compare this with series, where the current was shared and the voltage was divided. In parallel the voltage is shared by every branch, which leaves the current free to differ from branch to branch. Working out those currents comes next.

steps.headline: Each branch draws its own current

lead.text: With the full battery voltage across a branch, Ohm's law gives the current in it directly: the voltage divided by that branch's own resistance. A 12 V battery across a 40 Ω branch pushes 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 A through it. Across a 120 Ω branch it pushes 12 ÷ 120 = 0.1 A.

Adding a branch does not disturb the ones already there. The 40 Ω branch still has 12 V across it, so it still carries 0.3 A whether or not the 120 Ω branch is connected. This is the opposite of series, where a new resistor changed the current in every part.
So a branch has a current of its own, set by its resistance, and the smallest resistance carries the largest current. What the battery must supply in total is the next question.

steps.headline: The battery supplies every branch

lead.text: Charge leaving the battery reaches a point where the wire splits, and some of it goes down each branch. A water pipe that forks into two pipes behaves in the same way. The branches join up again on the far side, so the flow comes back together before it returns to the battery.

Charge cannot pile up or vanish at the split, so the amount that flows in from the battery each second equals the amount that flows out into the branches each second. The battery's current is the sum of the branch currents. With branches of 0.3 A and 0.1 A, the battery delivers 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4 A.
Every extra branch asks the battery for more current. The voltage across each branch stays the same, and a battery that feeds more lamps runs down faster.

steps.headline: The equivalent resistance

lead.text: From the battery's side, the two branches together are a load that draws some total current at some voltage. We can swap them for one resistor that draws the same total current from the same voltage. That single resistor is called the equivalent resistance of the branches.

Ohm's law finds it for the whole: the equivalent resistance is the battery voltage divided by the total current. For the 12 V battery across 40 Ω and 120 Ω, the total current was 0.4 A, so the equivalent resistance is 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 Ω.

That 30 Ω is smaller than either branch. It has to be, because the second branch gives the charge an extra route and the battery delivers more current than the first branch would take alone. Adding a branch always lowers the equivalent resistance, whereas adding a resistor in series raised the total.

steps.headline: A rule that needs only the resistances

lead.text: Finding the equivalent resistance through the currents works, but there is a shortcut that needs only the resistances. Write the total current as V ÷ R₁ + V ÷ R₂, and set it equal to V ÷ R, where R is the equivalent resistance. Every term has a V in it, so V cancels and leaves 1 ÷ R = 1 ÷ R₁ + 1 ÷ R₂.

So you add the reciprocals of the branch resistances, then flip the answer over. For 40 Ω and 120 Ω, 1 ÷ 40 + 1 ÷ 120 = 3 ÷ 120 + 1 ÷ 120 = 4 ÷ 120 = 1 ÷ 30. Flipping gives 30 Ω, the value we found from the currents.

Two equal branches make a quick special case. With two 10 Ω branches, 1 ÷ 10 + 1 ÷ 10 = 2 ÷ 10, which flips to 5 Ω, half of one branch. In any parallel pair the result is smaller than the smaller branch.
Use the reciprocal rule, then flip the result.

reveal.text: Two equal branches halve the resistance: the conductance doubles, so the resistance falls to half.

lessons.title: How much energy a circuit moves

steps.headline: A volt is energy for each coulomb

lead.text: A battery does more than push charge round. It gives each bit of charge some energy, which the charge carries round the loop and hands over to the parts it passes through. Energy is measured in joules, written J. Lifting a small apple, about 100 g, up by a metre takes roughly one joule.
This is what the volt measures. A 4 V battery gives every coulomb of charge that passes through it 4 joules, and a 9 V battery gives each coulomb 9 joules. One volt is one joule for each coulomb.
Voltage tells us the energy each coulomb carries, and current tells us how many coulombs pass each second. Put the two together and we can count the energy leaving the battery every second.

steps.headline: Power is energy each second

lead.text: The energy moved each second has its own name. Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, and it is measured in watts, written W. One watt is one joule each second, so a 5 W lamp transfers 5 joules every second.

Now put the battery's numbers to work. Each coulomb carries V joules, and I coulombs pass each second, so the energy delivered each second is V × I joules. That gives the formula P = I × V. Current in amperes times voltage in volts gives power in watts. A current of 0.2 A at 5 V is a power of 0.2 × 5 = 1 W.
Small currents are often quoted in milliamperes, written mA. One milliampere is 0.001 A, so convert to amperes before you multiply.

steps.headline: Power when you know the resistance

lead.text: Often you know a part's resistance and only one of its current or voltage. Ohm's law lets you rewrite the formula in terms of whichever two quantities you do have. Put V = I × R into P = I × V and you get P = I² × R. Put I = V ÷ R into P = I × V and you get P = V² ÷ R.
Check all three on a 48 Ω resistor with 12 V across it. Its current is 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 A, so P = 0.25 × 12 = 3 W. The other forms agree: V² ÷ R = 144 ÷ 48 = 3 W, and I² × R = 0.0625 × 48 = 3 W.
All three forms are the same law. Choose the one that uses the two numbers in front of you and you skip the step of finding the third.
You know a voltage and a resistance this time. Pick the form of the formula that uses exactly those.

reveal.text: With voltage and resistance, P = V² ÷ R skips the current. Finding the current first and using P = I × V gives the same answer.

steps.headline: Where the power goes

lead.text: In a resistor the energy that arrives is turned into heat, and the resistor warms up. The power tells you how fast that heating happens. A resistor asked to turn energy into heat faster than it can shed it gets too hot and can be damaged.

That is why resistors carry a power rating. The small resistors in a hobby kit are commonly rated at a quarter of a watt, 0.25 W. On 3 V a 100 Ω resistor transfers 9 ÷ 100 = 0.09 W, well within that rating. On 9 V it would transfer 81 ÷ 100 = 0.81 W, which is over three times the rating.

Work out the power before building a circuit and you can choose parts that stay cool. Power is a rate, though, so it does not yet say how much energy is moved in total. That depends on how long the circuit runs.

steps.headline: Energy is power multiplied by time

lead.text: A rate becomes a total when you multiply by time. A 5 W lamp transfers 5 joules each second, so in 10 seconds it transfers 5 × 10 = 50 J. In symbols E = P × t, with the energy E in joules, the power P in watts and the time t in seconds.

Power and energy are different things. Power is how fast energy moves, as speed is how fast a car goes. Energy is how much has moved, as distance is how far the car has gone. A lamp left on twice as long transfers twice the energy at an unchanged power.
If the power is not given, find it first. A lamp with 9 V across it and 0.1 A through it has a power of 0.1 × 9 = 0.9 W, and after 30 seconds it has transferred 0.9 × 30 = 27 J.

blocks.text: Touch a torch bulb that has been on for a few minutes and it is hot. The battery has been handing energy to the bulb, and the bulb has been turning it into light and heat. A battery that has powered the torch for long enough runs flat, because the energy it held has all gone.

A circuit moves energy from its battery to its parts, and how fast it does so decides how hot a bulb gets and how long a battery lasts. That rate is a number we can calculate from things we have already met, the current and the voltage.

We start by saying what a volt really measures, since that links a battery's push to energy. That gives a rule for how fast a circuit moves energy, and a second look using Ohm's law shows how the rule changes with the resistance. The last step turns the rate into the total energy moved in a minute.

lessons.title: Components that break the pattern

steps.headline: Parts that follow a straight line

lead.text: Take a 50 Ω resistor and raise the voltage across it a volt at a time. By Ohm's law the current is 0.02 A at 1 V, 0.04 A at 2 V, 0.06 A at 3 V and 0.08 A at 4 V. Each extra volt adds the same extra 0.02 A, so doubling the voltage doubles the current.

Plot those points on a graph, with voltage along the bottom and current up the side, and they fall on a straight line through the origin, the point where both are zero. A part that behaves like this is called ohmic, which means its resistance stays the same whatever the voltage. Ohm's law applies to it at every voltage, and one resistance value describes it completely.
That makes a resistor very easy to predict. Some parts keep no fixed resistance, though, and for them you cannot divide the voltage by one number and expect it to hold.

steps.headline: Diodes pass current one way

lead.text: A diode is a part that lets current through in one direction only. Its circuit symbol is a triangle pointing at a bar, and the point of the triangle shows the direction in which current can pass. Connect a diode the other way round and it blocks, so almost no current flows.
An LED is a light-emitting diode, a diode that gives out light when current passes through it. That is why an LED has a right way round: a reversed LED stays dark, and nothing is wrong with it.

A diode cannot be described by a single resistance, because the same voltage can give a current or none at all depending on which way it is connected. What happens in the allowed direction as the voltage grows is the next thing to look at.

lead.text: An LED is wired into a small battery circuit, with its two connections swapped.

reveal.text: A diode passes current one way only. Reversed, it blocks, so the circuit carries almost nothing.

steps.headline: Current climbs steeply past the forward voltage

lead.text: Now connect the diode the way it likes and raise the voltage across it slowly from zero. For a while almost nothing happens and the current stays near zero. Then, at a voltage that depends on the diode, the current starts to climb steeply, and a very small further rise in voltage makes it many times larger.

That voltage is called the forward voltage. For a red LED it is about 2 V, and for a blue LED about 3 V. Once the LED is conducting, the voltage across it stays close to that value whatever the current. A graph of its current against voltage is a curve that bends sharply upwards. It is not a straight line, so the LED is not ohmic.

That is a problem for anyone who wants to run an LED from a battery. The LED does not limit its own current, and too much current damages it. Something else in the circuit has to set the current, and we already know a part whose job is exactly that.

diagram.alt: A graph of current against voltage for LEDs. The current stays near zero, then climbs steeply past the forward voltage, about 2 volts for a red LED and about 3 volts for a blue one. A resistor gives a straight line instead.
diagram.caption: The LED's current stays near zero, then climbs steeply past its forward voltage. It is not a straight line, so the LED is not ohmic.

steps.headline: A series resistor sets the current

lead.text: The answer is a resistor in series with the LED. Both sit on one path, so the same current passes through each, and as in the series lesson the voltage drops around the loop add up to the battery's voltage. The LED takes its forward voltage and the resistor takes whatever is left.

The leftover voltage and the current you want fix the resistor through Ohm's law. Take a 5 V supply and a red LED with a 2 V forward voltage that should carry 10 mA. The resistor has 5 − 2 = 3 V across it. Ten milliamperes is 0.01 A, so R = 3 ÷ 0.01 = 300 Ω.
A different resistor gives a different current, which is exactly the control the LED lacked. The next screens take the same steps with other numbers.

diagram.alt: A 5 volt battery, a resistor and an LED in series with a meter. The LED keeps 2 volts and the resistor takes the other 3 volts. A 300 ohm resistor gives 10 milliamperes and a 600 ohm resistor gives 5 milliamperes.
diagram.caption: The LED keeps its forward voltage and the resistor takes the rest. A different resistor gives a different current.

blocks.text: A 50 Ω resistor carries 0.02 A when it has 1 V across it. Raise the voltage to 2 V and Ohm's law says the current doubles, to 0.04 A. Every part in this course so far has behaved that way, which makes the sums pleasantly predictable.

Not every part plays along. A small indicator light of the kind on the front of so many gadgets is different. At low voltage it carries almost nothing, and then past a certain voltage the current through it shoots up. Connect one straight across a battery and it can burn out in moments, so every such light in a working gadget comes with a resistor chosen by someone who did the calculation in this lesson.
We begin by saying what it means to follow Ohm's law and what that looks like on a graph. Then we meet a part that breaks the pattern, and a short calculation sizes the resistor that keeps it safe.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a part that follows Ohm's law from one that doesn't, and choose the resistor that protects an indicator light.

recap.keyIdea: An ohmic part keeps a constant resistance. An LED does not: it passes current one way and climbs steeply past its forward voltage, so a series resistor sets the current.

blocks.text: You found that a 5 V supply, a 2 V LED and 15 mA need a 200 Ω resistor, and that doubling the voltage on a resistor doubles its current.

recap.nextHook: That completes the basics of direct-current circuits, and going back through the course shows which rule fits which circuit.

The current doubles because the path is shorter
The diode lights more brightly and cools down

questions.onCorrect: A diode passes current one way only, so a reversed LED stays dark.

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing a diode matters: it is a one-way component.
A shorter path isn't the issue. Think about which way a diode passes current.
A reversed diode can't conduct better. It is a one-way component.

questions.prompt: Two 100 Ω branches are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
hints: Start with the sum of reciprocals.
Substitute 100 Ω for both branches.
Add the two reciprocal terms, then invert the result.
questions.onCorrect: 50 Ω. Two equal routes halve the resistance, because the conductance doubles.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the resistances, which is the series rule. Branches add reciprocals.
That is the sum of the reciprocals. Invert it to get back to ohms.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply feeds two branches, which carry 0.12 A and 0.04 A. What total current does the supply deliver, in amperes?
hints: The supply feeds both branches.
Combine the two branch currents.
Add 0.12 and 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branch currents are 12 / 100 = 0.12 A and 12 / 300 = 0.04 A. Their sum is 0.16 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.16 A. The supply delivers every branch's current together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only one branch. The supply delivers both.
Branch currents are not averaged. The supply provides all of them.

questions.prompt: Why is the equivalent resistance of parallel branches smaller than either branch on its own?
hints: Think about what adding a branch gives charge.
Ask what happens to the total current the supply delivers.
Relate that extra current to the resistance the supply sees.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A second branch gives charge another route, so the supply delivers more current for the same voltage. That is why the equivalent resistance is smaller than either branch.

questions.onCorrect: A second branch is another route, so the supply delivers more current and the resistance it sees falls.

questions.prompt: Two lamps are wired as separate routes across a 6 V battery. What is the voltage across each lamp, in volts?
hints: Look at where each lamp connects. Both have one end on each battery terminal.
Compare each lamp's two ends with the battery's two terminals.
Does the battery's voltage get shared out, or does each lamp connect straight across it?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both lamps connect across the same two battery terminals, so each has the full 6 V.

questions.onCorrect: 6 V each. Branches span the same two points, so each has the full voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: The voltage is not shared out between branches. Each lamp connects directly across the battery.
There is only one battery. Each lamp is connected across it, not across two batteries.

questions.prompt: A resistor carries 0.02 A with 2 V across it. What current does it carry with 4 V across it, in amperes?
hints: Use Ohm's law to find the resistance first.
2 V and 0.02 A give a resistance of 100 Ω.
Now divide 4 V by that resistance.
questions.onCorrect: 0.04 A. The resistance stays 100 Ω, so double the voltage gives double the current.

misconceptions.feedback: The current changes when the voltage does. Find the resistance, then use it at the new voltage.

questions.prompt: A resistor is ohmic. What does its graph of current against voltage look like?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: A straight line through the origin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straight line through the origin

choices.label: A straight line through the origin
A curve that bends upwards
A flat line

questions.onCorrect: A straight line through the origin: constant resistance means current proportional to voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: A bend means the resistance changes with voltage. That is not an ohmic component.
A flat line would mean the current ignores the voltage.

questions.prompt: The arrow in a diode's circuit symbol points from left to right. Which way can current go through it?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Left to right only

choices.label: Left to right only
Right to left only
Either way

questions.onCorrect: Left to right only: the arrow shows the one direction a diode passes.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow points the way the diode passes current, not the way it blocks.
A diode is a one-way component. It does not pass current both ways.

questions.prompt: The voltage across an LED rises slowly from 0 V. What does its current do?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply

choices.label: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
Rises in a straight line, like a resistor's
Falls as the voltage rises

questions.onCorrect: Near zero, then a steep climb past the forward voltage: an LED does not follow a straight line.

misconceptions.feedback: A straight line is what a resistor does. An LED is different.
More voltage does not lower the current in a forward-biased LED.

questions.prompt: Why does the series resistor get the voltage the LED leaves over?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply

choices.label: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
The LED switches the resistor on
Resistors always take 2 V

questions.onCorrect: Series voltage drops add to the supply, so the resistor takes what the LED does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The LED doesn't switch anything. Think about how voltage drops in series add up.
The resistor's voltage depends on the supply and the LED. It is not fixed.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery lights a blue LED with a forward voltage of 3 V at 10 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The LED keeps its forward voltage. How much of the supply is left?
Divide that leftover voltage by the current, in amperes.
10 mA is 0.01 A. Work out the leftover voltage divided by 0.01.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 9 V − 3 V = 6 V. R = 6 V ÷ 0.01 A = 600 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 600 Ω. Take off the forward voltage, then divide what's left by the current.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the whole 9 V. The LED keeps its forward voltage; the resistor gets the rest.
Check the units. The current is in milliamperes, so convert it to amperes first.

questions.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 12 V supply at 25 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: Subtract the LED's forward voltage from the supply.
Convert 25 mA to amperes.
Divide the leftover voltage by 0.025.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 12 V − 2 V = 10 V. R = 10 V ÷ 0.025 A = 400 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 400 Ω. The resistor takes the leftover voltage and sets the current.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the whole supply voltage. The LED keeps its forward voltage.
Check the units. Convert milliamperes to amperes before dividing.

questions.prompt: How many litres pass a mark after the narrow section each second?
hints: Where could the water go if the pipe doesn't leak?
If more arrived than left, what would pile up?
Whatever passes the first mark each second must also pass the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing leaks and nothing builds up, so 2 litres pass the second mark each second.

questions.onCorrect: 2 litres. Nothing leaks or piles up in a closed loop, so the flow is the same at every mark.

misconceptions.feedback: Water would have to vanish in the narrow part. Where would the missing water go?
The pump keeps pushing, so some water always passes. Think about what the narrow section can and can't do.

questions.prompt: A single loop holds a battery and one resistor. A meter just before the resistor reads 0.05 A. What does an identical meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: Think of the water in the pipe: did the count change after the narrow neck?
Could any charge leave the wire inside the resistor, or be stored there?
Count the routes the charge has around the loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One path, so the current is the same on both sides: 0.05 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.05 A. One path means one current: every point on the loop passes the same charge each second.

misconceptions.feedback: A resistor holds the flow back but the loop is still carrying current. What would happen to charge that stopped arriving?
Half would mean charge vanished in the resistor. A resistor limits the flow of the whole loop; it does not consume charge.

questions.prompt: Why does Ohm's law divide the voltage by the resistance?
hints: Think about what a bigger resistance does to the flow.
If R grows, should the current grow or shrink?

acceptedIdeas: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current.

choices.label: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
A bigger resistance pushes harder, so it gives a bigger current
Resistance and voltage are measured in the same unit

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by R makes a bigger resistance give a smaller current. That is what opposition means.

misconceptions.feedback: Resistance opposes the flow; it does not push. Ask which way the current should move when R grows.
Volts and ohms are different units. The question is about what resistance does to the flow.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a loop with one 60 Ω resistor. What does a meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: What does Ohm's law give for the whole loop?
In a single loop the current is the same at every point.
Work out 12 ÷ 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 60 Ω = 0.2 A, and the current is the same on both sides of the resistor.

questions.onCorrect: 0.2 A. Ohm's law gives the loop's current, and the same current passes every point in it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the voltage by the resistance. A resistor lowers the current, so the answer should be small.
You divided the resistance by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.

questions.prompt: A 10 V supply drives a single loop containing one 400 Ω resistor. Calculate the current, in amperes.
hints: Which value goes on top in Ohm's law?
Divide the supply voltage by the resistance.
Work out 10 ÷ 400. It is less than 0.1.
questions.onCorrect: 0.025 A. Voltage over resistance, and 400 Ω is a lot of opposition for 10 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.
That multiplies the two values. More resistance means less current.

questions.prompt: What does current measure?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: How much charge passes a point each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much charge passes a point each second

choices.label: How much charge passes a point each second
How much charge is stored in the wire
How hard the battery pushes

questions.onCorrect: Current is a rate: charge passing a point each second, in amperes.

misconceptions.feedback: Current is not stored in the wire. It is charge moving past a point.
How hard the battery pushes is the voltage. Current is the flow that results.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the current?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: V ÷ R

choices.label: V ÷ R
V × R
R ÷ V

questions.onCorrect: Voltage divided by resistance: a bigger resistance gives a smaller current.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying would make more resistance give more current. Resistance holds the current back.
That puts the resistance on top. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.

questions.prompt: A loop with a 6 V battery and one resistor carries 0.02 A. The resistor is swapped for one with half the resistance. What is the current now, in amperes?
hints: Does halving the resistance make the current rise or fall?
Find the resistance of the first resistor, then halve it.
The first resistor was 300 Ω, so the new one is 150 Ω. Work out 6 ÷ 150.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R = 6 V ÷ 0.02 A = 300 Ω. Half of that is 150 Ω, so I = 6 V ÷ 150 Ω = 0.04 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.04 A. Half the resistance means twice the current, because resistance sits under the division.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving the resistance does not halve the current. A weaker hold-back lets more charge through.
That is the current before the swap. The resistance has changed, so the current has too.

questions.prompt: A battery gives each coulomb of charge 4 joules. Each second, 0.5 coulombs pass through it. How many joules does the battery deliver each second?
hints: Each coulomb brings 4 joules. How many coulombs pass in one second?
Half a coulomb brings half of 4 joules.
Work out 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each second 0.5 coulombs pass, each carrying 4 J: 0.5 × 4 = 2 J.

questions.onCorrect: 2 J each second. Energy per coulomb times coulombs per second gives energy per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 0.5. Half a coulomb carries less energy than a whole one, so the answer is smaller than 4.
Adding mixes two different things. Each coulomb brings energy, so scale that energy by how many coulombs pass.

questions.prompt: Which resistor transfers more power?
hints: Power uses both current and voltage.
Work out the product for each resistor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They transfer the same power: 0.5 A × 8 V and 2 A × 2 V both give 4 W.

choices.label: The first, with 0.5 A and 8 V
The second, with 2 A and 2 V
They transfer the same power

questions.onCorrect: Same power: both products come to 4 W. Neither current nor voltage alone tells you how hard a component works.

misconceptions.feedback: It has more voltage but less current. Compare the products, not one number at a time.
It has more current but less voltage. Compare the products, not one number at a time.

questions.prompt: Why can you multiply the current by the voltage to find power?
hints: Think back to the coulombs and joules on the first screen.
What units does the product of coulombs per second and joules per coulomb have?

acceptedIdeas: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second, so the product is energy per second.

choices.label: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
Multiplying always gives the larger of the two numbers
Current and voltage are two names for the same thing

questions.onCorrect: Joules per coulomb times coulombs per second is joules per second, which is watts.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying doesn't pick the larger number. Think about what each quantity measures.
They are different quantities. One counts charge passing, the other measures the energy each charge carries.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 0.2 A through a lamp for 60 s. How much energy does the lamp transfer, in joules?
hints: Find the power first, from the current and the voltage.
Power is energy each second. How many seconds does the lamp run?
Multiply the power by the 60 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 108 J. Power gives joules each second, and the lamp runs for 60 of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power, joules each second. The lamp runs for a whole minute.
Power is already a rate, so you multiply by time, not divide.
That leaves out the voltage. Find the power first.

questions.prompt: A 50 Ω resistor carries 0.1 A. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: You know the current and the resistance, not the voltage.
Find the voltage across the resistor with V = IR, or use P = I²R.
Square the current, then multiply by the resistance.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 W. With current and resistance, P = I²R gives the power directly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the voltage across the resistor. Power needs one more step.
That is the current squared. Multiply by the resistance as well.

questions.prompt: A heater transfers 100 joules of energy every second. What is its power, in watts?
hints: A watt is one joule each second.
How many joules each second does the heater transfer?
Read the power straight from the joules each second.
questions.onCorrect: 100 W. A watt is one joule each second.

misconceptions.feedback: A watt is one joule each second, so the number is not divided down.
Power in joules each second needs no extra multiplying.

questions.prompt: You know a resistor's voltage and its resistance. Which expression gives its power?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: V² ÷ R

choices.label: V² ÷ R
I² × R
V ÷ R

questions.onCorrect: V² ÷ R. It uses exactly the two quantities you know.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs the current, which you don't have yet.
That is the current, not the power.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives 0.12 A through a 100 Ω resistor. A second 100 Ω resistor is wired straight across the same two battery terminals, as a separate route. What total current does the battery supply now, in amperes?
hints: Does the first resistor notice the second? It still has the full battery across it.
Work out the current in the second resistor with Ohm's law.
The battery supplies both routes, so combine the two currents.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each resistor still has 12 V across it, so each carries 0.12 A. The battery supplies both: 0.24 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.24 A. Each route carries its own current from the full battery voltage, and the battery supplies both.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one resistor's current. The battery now supplies the second route too.
The first resistor still has the full battery across it, so it keeps its current. A new route adds to it.

questions.prompt: Why does the 20 Ω branch have the full 6 V across it?
hints: Where does each branch connect?
Compare its two ends with the supply's terminals.

acceptedIdeas: Both branches connect across the same two points as the supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both branches connect across the same two points as the supply.

choices.label: Both branches connect across the same two points as the supply
The 20 Ω branch is nearer the battery
The 30 Ω branch uses up its voltage first

questions.onCorrect: Each branch connects across the same two points as the supply, so each gets the supply's voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance along the wire doesn't change a branch's voltage. Ask where each branch's ends connect.
Branches don't take voltage from each other. Ask where each branch's ends connect.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery powers a 90 Ω lamp. A 45 Ω lamp is added as another branch. What total current does the battery supply, in amperes?
hints: Each lamp has the full 9 V across it.
Find each lamp's current with Ohm's law.
Work out 9 ÷ 90 and 9 ÷ 45, then combine them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lamps carry 9 ÷ 90 = 0.1 A and 9 ÷ 45 = 0.2 A. Total: 0.3 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.3 A. Each branch takes its own current from the full voltage, and the battery supplies both.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one lamp. The battery supplies both branches.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply is connected across a 30 Ω branch and a 60 Ω branch. What total current does it deliver, in amperes?
hints: Each branch has the full 12 V across it.
Find each branch current with Ohm's law.
Work out 12 ÷ 30 and 12 ÷ 60, then combine them.
questions.onCorrect: 0.6 A. Each branch takes its own current, and the supply delivers them together.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one branch. The supply delivers both.
That treats the branches as one path in series. Branches take their own currents.

questions.prompt: What is the equivalent resistance of a 30 Ω branch and a 60 Ω branch in parallel, in ohms?
hints: Add the reciprocals, not the resistances.
Invert the total of the reciprocals.
questions.onCorrect: 20 Ω. Add the reciprocals, then invert. The result is below the smaller branch.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the resistances, which is the series rule.
That is the sum of the reciprocals. Invert it to get ohms.

questions.prompt: A third lamp is added as another branch across the same battery. What happens to the voltage across the first lamp?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays the same

choices.label: It stays the same
It falls, because the battery is shared
It rises

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Each branch connects directly across the supply.

misconceptions.feedback: Branches don't share out the voltage. Each one connects directly across the battery.
Adding a branch does not push more voltage across the others.

questions.prompt: A 50 Ω branch is joined in parallel with a 200 Ω branch. The equivalent resistance is:
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Less than 50 Ω

choices.label: Less than 50 Ω
Between 50 Ω and 200 Ω

questions.onCorrect: Less than 50 Ω. Another route always lowers the equivalent resistance.

misconceptions.feedback: Another route can only make it easier for charge. The result can't sit between the two.
That adds the resistances, which is the series rule.

questions.prompt: A 10 V battery drives 0.1 A through one 100 Ω resistor. A second 100 Ω resistor joins the same wire, one after the other. What is the current now, in amperes?
hints: Two resistors in a row hold the flow back more than one.
Ohm's law still gives the current as V ÷ R. What is R now?
Treat the pair as one 200 Ω resistor and divide.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two resistors oppose the flow like 200 Ω, so I = 10 V ÷ 200 Ω = 0.05 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.05 A. The second resistor doubles the opposition, so the same battery drives half the current.

misconceptions.feedback: Two resistors oppose the flow more than one, so the current should fall, not rise.
That is the current with one resistor. The second one adds opposition.

questions.prompt: A meter beside the 100 Ω resistor reads 0.03 A. What does a meter beside the 200 Ω resistor read, in amperes?
hints: How many routes does charge have around this loop?
Could charge leave the path between the two resistors?
Recall what you found about current in a single loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One path, so the same current passes both resistors: 0.03 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.03 A. A single path carries a single current, whatever the resistors are.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger resistance holds the flow back for the whole loop. It does not use current up on its own side.
The larger resistor does not make more charge pass. One path means one current.

questions.prompt: Why do series resistances add?
hints: Think about the route the charge takes.
Does the charge meet one resistor or both?

acceptedIdeas: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn.

choices.label: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn
Each resistor has a battery of its own
The resistors share the current equally

questions.onCorrect: Charge meets the resistors one after another, so their opposition builds up along the single path.

misconceptions.feedback: There is one battery in the loop. Ask what the charge meets as it goes round.
Sharing current is true, but it doesn't explain adding. Think about what the charge passes through on its way round.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a 100 Ω resistor and a 200 Ω resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 200 Ω resistor, in volts?
hints: Find the total resistance first, then the current.
The voltage across a resistor is the current times its own resistance.
The current is 12 ÷ 300. Multiply it by 200.
questions.onCorrect: 8 V. The larger resistor takes the larger share, and the two shares add back to 12 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of the smaller resistor. Check which resistor the question asks about.
The battery's voltage isn't split equally. A bigger resistance takes a bigger share.
That is the current. The question asks for the voltage across the 200 Ω resistor.

questions.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected to a 100 Ω resistor and a 500 Ω resistor in series. Calculate the current, in amperes.
hints: Add the two resistances first.
Divide the battery voltage by that total.
Work out 6 ÷ 600.
questions.onCorrect: 0.01 A. Add the resistances, then let Ohm's law work on the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only the 100 Ω resistor. Both resistors are in the path.
That uses only the 500 Ω resistor. Both resistors are in the path.

questions.prompt: What is the total resistance of a 10 Ω and a 20 Ω resistor in series, in ohms?
hints: Resistors in series add.
Write R1 + R2 with the two values.
Add 10 and 20.
questions.onCorrect: 30 Ω. In series the resistances add.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one resistor's value. Both are in the path, so both count.
That multiplies the two values. Series resistances add.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery drives two resistors in series. One has 5 V across it. How many volts are across the other?
hints: The two drops add back to the battery's voltage.
Take the known drop away from the supply.
Work out 9 − 5.
questions.onCorrect: 4 V. The voltage drops add back to the battery's 9 V.

misconceptions.feedback: The drops are not equal here. They add to the battery's voltage.
The whole battery voltage is shared between the two. Neither resistor gets all of it.

flashcards.front: What does Ohm's law relate, and how is it written?
flashcards.back: For an ohmic component it fixes the current as the voltage divided by the resistance: I = V / R.

flashcards.front: What does electric current measure, and in what unit?
flashcards.back: The rate at which electric charge passes a point, measured in amperes.

flashcards.front: How is the equivalent resistance of resistors in series calculated?
flashcards.back: By adding them: Rtotal = R1 + R2, and so on for any further resistors in the path.

flashcards.front: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same in every component?
flashcards.back: The current, because a series path does not divide.

flashcards.front: How is the electrical power of a component calculated from its current and voltage?
flashcards.back: P = IV, in watts. Substituting Ohm's law also gives P = I²R and P = V² / R.

flashcards.front: What separates electrical power from electrical energy?
flashcards.back: Power is the rate of energy transfer; energy is that power multiplied by the time the circuit runs.

flashcards.front: Why does a light-emitting diode need a resistor in series with it?
flashcards.back: Its current rises steeply past the forward voltage, so the resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current.

flashcards.front: What does it mean to call a component ohmic?
flashcards.back: Its current stays proportional to the voltage across it, so its resistance is constant.

flashcards.front: What happens to equivalent resistance when branches are connected in parallel?
flashcards.back: It falls below the resistance of the smallest branch because the branch conductances add.

flashcards.front: What potential difference does each parallel branch have?
flashcards.back: Each branch has the same potential difference because every branch connects across the same two points.
